opus-5.5.text:
I think there isn't one fixed ratio. It depends a lot on what stage your team is at and what bottleneck you're facing. But I do have a few principles I believe in.

First, I think research compute is the most underestimated. Many teams, especially when they're under pressure to ship a model, put almost everything into the big pre-training run and leave very little for exploration. In the short term that looks efficient, but in the long run it's very dangerous. Most of the real leaps, whether a new architecture, a better data recipe, or a new training paradigm, come from many small-scale experiments, and most of those fail. If researchers have to queue for weeks to run an ablation, the iteration speed of the whole organization slows down. So I'd rather guarantee a meaningful, stable share for research, maybe something like a quarter to a third, and protect it so it doesn't get squeezed every time a big run needs more.

Second, for pre-training, I think the key isn't just how many GPUs you give it, but whether you've de-risked it before you launch. A large pre-training run is very expensive, and you basically only get one shot at that scale. So the research compute should serve pre-training: you validate scaling behavior, data mixtures, and stability at smaller scales first, and only when you're confident do you commit the big cluster. Pre-training will still take the largest single block, but it should be a well-prepared bet, not a gamble.

Third, post-training's share has clearly been growing, and I think it will keep growing. Especially with reinforcement learning and reasoning, the compute you spend after pre-training can bring very large capability gains. RL is also quite compute-hungry, because of rollouts, inference, and many iterations. A few years ago people treated post-training as a small finishing step. Now I think it's closer to a second main phase of training, and allocation should reflect that.

So if I had to summarize: protect research so the team keeps learning, make pre-training a carefully validated big bet, and take post-training much more seriously than before. And the allocation should be dynamic. Leaders need to keep adjusting based on where the marginal return of compute is highest at that moment, rather than fixing a ratio once and never revisiting it.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training gets the largest single block and post-training’s share is growing, but it does not recommend roughly equal compute for the two.

r002.rationale: It recommends protecting roughly a quarter to a third for research and says pre-training gets the largest single block; it does not recommend more GPUs for research than for pre-training and post-training combined.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question every lab fights over internally, and I don't think there's one right split. But I can say how I've come to think about it.

The first thing is that these three aren't really the same kind of resource consumer. Pre-training is lumpy. When you commit to a big run, it eats the majority of your cluster for weeks or months, and you can't really pause it halfway without wasting what you've already spent. Post-training and research are much more elastic. They want many small to medium jobs, lots of iteration, fast turnaround. So the honest answer is that it's less about a fixed percentage and more about a schedule: when is a big run happening, and what does the cluster look like in between.

That said, if you force me to give a number, I'd say research should get a protected floor that nobody is allowed to touch, something like 15 to 20 percent. The reason is that research is the thing that gets squeezed first when deadlines hit, and it's also the thing that determines whether your next pre-training run is actually better or just bigger. If you starve the people doing scaling law experiments, architecture ablations, data mixture studies, then six months later you launch an expensive run on gut feeling. The cost of that mistake is far higher than the GPUs you saved.

Pre-training then takes the big block when a run is live, and the rest of the time that capacity should flow to post-training and research rather than sitting idle. One mistake I've seen is treating post-training as cheap. It isn't anymore. Reinforcement learning, especially with long reasoning traces, consumes a surprising amount of compute, and the evaluation loops around it are also expensive. A lot of the gap between a decent base model and a model people actually want to use comes from that stage, so it deserves real allocation, not leftovers.

The last point is about who decides. I don't think it should be purely top-down, and it definitely shouldn't be whoever shouts loudest in the meeting. You want a small group that has actually trained models looking at concrete proposals: what are you going to learn, what does success look like, what's the smallest scale that would still tell you something. Many research questions can be answered at a fraction of the size people initially ask for. Being disciplined about that frees up far more compute than any clever scheduling trick.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no fixed split and describes pre-training as taking a big block during runs, while post-training deserves real allocation. It does not recommend roughly equal compute investment in the two.

r002.rationale: It recommends a protected 15–20% floor for research, but does not say research should receive more GPUs than pre-training and post-training combined.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the bottleneck rather than a fixed ratio. Pre-training needs concentrated compute for a sustained run, while research needs room for smaller experiments that may or may not work. If you allocate everything to the next big training run, you can end up repeating the same approach without learning how to improve it.

So I’d protect a research budget, commit enough GPUs to make pre-training runs productive, and allocate post-training compute according to what we’re learning from evaluations. If the model has the underlying capability but isn’t using it reliably, post-training deserves more attention. If the capability itself is missing, we need to investigate the data and pre-training approach.

The allocation should change as the project develops. The important thing is to keep experiments feeding into the next decision, rather than treating the GPU split as something you set once.

r001.rationale: It recommends adjusting post-training compute based on evaluation results, but does not recommend roughly equal investment in pre-training and post-training.

r002.rationale: It recommends protecting a research budget, but does not say research should receive more GPUs than pre-training and post-training combined.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think there’s a fixed ratio that works for every team. I’d start with the bottleneck: are we limited by the base model’s capabilities, or are we failing to bring out capabilities it already has?

Pre-training needs a substantial, stable allocation because large runs require continuity. Post-training should have enough compute for fast iteration, especially when improvements depend on generating samples and testing them. And I would protect a portion for research, so exploratory work doesn’t get squeezed out by the next production deadline.

The key is to reassess the allocation as you learn. Run smaller experiments, understand which direction is producing meaningful gains, and then scale it. The goal isn’t to keep every GPU busy; it’s to make sure the compute is answering the most important questions.

r001.rationale: It recommends a stable allocation for pre-training and enough compute for post-training, but does not say to invest roughly equally in the two.

r002.rationale: It recommends protecting some compute for research, but does not say research should receive more GPUs than pre-training and post-training combined.
